prompt: Why does the section call D_2 + F → DF + D a rebound reaction?

choices.text: Most DF molecules bounce back toward the general direction they came from
Most DF molecules carry on in the direction the reactants were moving
choices.why: Products carrying on forward mark a stripping reaction. In D_2 + F, the vast majority of DF bounce back the way they came.

choices.text: DF and D scatter equally forward and backward
choices.why: Scattering both forward and backward comes from a long-lived intermediate. D_2 + F sends most DF back toward where they came from.

choices.text: The F atom bounces off D_2 without reacting
choices.why: D_2 + F does react, forming DF. It is a rebound reaction because the DF product heads back in the general direction it came from.

explanation: In D_2 + F → DF + D, the vast majority of DF molecules bounce off the collision with D_2 back toward the general direction from which they came. That backward scattering is what makes it a rebound reaction.

choices.text: One in which most products continue in the direction the reactants were moving
One in which most products head back the way the reactants came
choices.why: That describes a rebound reaction, such as D_2 + F. In a stripping reaction the products carry on forward after the collision.

choices.text: One in which products scatter equally forward and backward
choices.why: That pattern comes from a meta-stable intermediate that rotates many times before splitting. In a stripping reaction most products move forward.

choices.text: One in which the collision strips electrons from both reactants
choices.why: Electron transfer does happen in the section's example, but from one reactant to the other, and the name refers to the scattering direction: the products keep moving forward.

explanation: In a stripping reaction, a majority of the product molecules continue moving after the collision in the same direction that the precursor reactant molecules were going. This is the opposite of a rebound reaction.

prompt: In the stripping reaction of K with I_2, in which direction does the KI product move off after the collision?

choices.text: In the same general direction as the incoming K atom
Back toward where the K atom came from
choices.why: Heading back would make it a rebound reaction. In this stripping reaction KI carries on in the direction K was moving.

choices.text: In the same general direction as the incoming I_2 molecule
choices.why: KI keeps the motion of the K atom it formed from. It moves off in the same general direction as the incoming K.

choices.text: Equally in all directions
choices.why: Even scattering is not what a stripping reaction gives. KI moves off in the same general direction as the incoming K atom.

explanation: After the collision, KI moves off in the same general direction as the incoming K atom. The product carries on forward, which is what makes K + I_2 a stripping reaction.

prompt: For stripping reactions, how does the experimental hard-sphere collision cross section generally compare with the theoretical estimate?

choices.text: It is larger
It is smaller
choices.why: A smaller cross section would mean fewer collisions react than the hard spheres allow. In stripping reactions, reaction happens over a larger area than the estimate.

choices.text: It is the same
choices.why: If they matched, no special explanation would be needed. The experimental cross section is larger, which the section explains by electron transfer before the collision.

choices.text: It is zero, since no collision takes place
choices.why: The reactants still collide and react. The point is that the measured cross section is larger than the hard-sphere estimate.

explanation: In stripping reactions, the experimental cross section is generally found to be larger than the theoretical hard-sphere estimate. It is so large that two particles could stay inside the collision area and still pass by each other without colliding.

prompt: The section says that in stripping reactions the experimental cross section is so large that two particles could remain inside the collision area and yet pass by each other without colliding. What does this suggest?

choices.text: Something draws the particles together before they come into contact
The particles are much smaller than their hard-sphere sizes
choices.why: Smaller particles would give a smaller cross section, not a larger one. Particles that would miss are being pulled together before contact.

choices.text: Most collisions inside the area fail to react
choices.why: A large experimental cross section means more encounters react, not fewer. Particles that would otherwise miss still end up reacting.

choices.text: The hard-sphere estimate is correct and the measurement is wrong
choices.why: The section takes the measurement as real and explains it: an electron transfers first, and the resulting ions attract each other.

explanation: In a hard-sphere picture, particles that pass each other without touching cannot react. The large measured cross section means they react anyway, because an electron transfers between them first and the resulting ions are drawn toward each other.

prompt: What has been found experimentally to happen in stripping reactions before the two particles collide?

choices.text: An electron transfers from one particle to the other
One particle breaks apart into atoms
choices.why: The reactants stay intact until they meet. What happens first is an electron transfer, which turns the two particles into ions.

choices.text: The particles form a long-lived complex that rotates many times
choices.why: A long-lived complex explains forward and backward scattering, not stripping. In stripping, an electron transfers before the particles collide.

choices.text: One particle becomes vibrationally excited
choices.why: The section's explanation of the large cross section is an electron transfer, not vibrational excitation. The ions formed then attract each other.

explanation: It has been determined experimentally that an electron transfers between the two particles before they collide. This produces a pair of oppositely charged ions.

prompt: After the electron transfer in a stripping reaction, what draws the two particles toward each other?

choices.text: The Coulomb attraction between the oppositely charged ions
The Coulomb repulsion between two like-charged ions
choices.why: The electron transfer leaves one particle positive and the other negative. Opposite charges attract, which pulls the ions together.

choices.text: A hard-sphere collision between the neutral particles
choices.why: After the transfer the particles are no longer neutral. The force between them is the Coulomb attraction of opposite charges, acting before contact.

choices.text: Gravity between the two particles
choices.why: The pull the section describes is electrical: the Coulomb potential created by the opposite charges of the two ions.

explanation: The electron transfer produces a positive ion and a negative ion. They are drawn toward each other by the Coulomb potential created by their opposite charges, which is why the reaction reaches beyond the hard-sphere cross section.

prompt: In the section's mechanism for the stripping reaction of K(g) with I_2(g), what is step 1?

choices.why: The charges are reversed. K gives up its electron and becomes K^+, while I_2 takes it and becomes I_2^−.
That is step 2, which uses the ions. They first have to be formed, by electron transfer from K to I_2 in step 1.
The mechanism doesn't begin by breaking I_2 apart. Step 1 is an electron transfer that forms K^+ and I_2^−.

explanation: Step 1 is the electron transfer: K(g) + I_2(g) → K^+(g) + I_2^−(g). It happens before the particles collide, and the ions it forms then attract each other.

prompt: In the section's mechanism for K(g) + I_2(g), which step follows the formation of K^+(g) and I_2^−(g)?

choices.why: That would just undo step 1. In step 2 the ions react to form the products KI and I.
The section's mechanism doesn't form a stable KI_2. In step 2 the ions give KI and a free I atom.
That doesn't conserve charge, and it isn't the section's step. In step 2 the ions give KI and an I atom.

explanation: Step 2 is K^+(g) + I_2^−(g) → KI(g) + I(g). Adding the two steps gives the overall reaction K + I_2 → KI + I, with K^+ and I_2^− as intermediates.

prompt: In the two-step mechanism K + I_2 → K^+ + I_2^− followed by K^+ + I_2^− → KI + I, which species are intermediates?

choices.text: K^+ and I_2^−
K and I_2
choices.why: These are the reactants: they are used up in step 1 and not formed again. The intermediates are formed in step 1 and used up in step 2.

choices.text: KI and I
choices.why: These are the products; they are formed in step 2 and not used up. The intermediates are the ions K^+ and I_2^−.

choices.text: K^+ only
choices.why: I_2^− is formed in step 1 and used up in step 2 just as K^+ is, so both ions are intermediates.

explanation: K^+ and I_2^− are made in step 1 and consumed in step 2, so neither appears in the overall reaction K + I_2 → KI + I. They are the ion pair that the Coulomb attraction draws together.

prompt: In the first step of the K + I_2 stripping reaction, which species gains the electron?

choices.text: I_2, which becomes I_2^−
K, which becomes K^−
choices.why: K gives up an electron rather than gaining one, becoming K^+. The electron goes to I_2.

choices.text: K, which becomes K^+
choices.why: K^+ is formed, but by losing an electron, not gaining one. The species that gains the electron is I_2.

choices.text: Neither; the step forms neutral atoms
choices.why: Step 1 produces ions, K^+ and I_2^−, not neutral atoms. The electron moves from K to I_2.

explanation: Step 1 is K(g) + I_2(g) → K^+(g) + I_2^−(g). K loses an electron and I_2 gains it, giving the oppositely charged pair that then attract.

prompt: In a crossed molecular beam experiment, a bimolecular reaction's products disperse in both the forward and reverse directions. What does the section say could explain this?

choices.text: A single atom-molecule structure that rotates many times before splitting
A simple hard-sphere collision
choices.why: The section says a simple hard-sphere model gives no explanation for this pattern. It needs a structure that survives long enough to rotate.

choices.text: An electron transfer before the collision
choices.why: Electron transfer explains the large cross sections of stripping reactions, where the products move mostly forward, not in both directions.

choices.text: A rebound off the far side of the molecule
choices.why: A rebound sends most products backward only. Products going both forward and backward point to a structure that rotates many times before breaking up.

explanation: If the colliding particles form a single atom-molecule structure that lasts long enough to undergo many rotations before splitting into products, it is reasonable for the products to scatter both forward and backward. The section calls these meta-stable intermediates.

prompt: According to the section, what can a simple hard-sphere collision model say about reactions whose products scatter both forward and backward?

choices.text: Nothing; it offers no explanation for that pattern
It predicts the pattern exactly
choices.why: The section says there is no explanation for this pattern if we insist on a simple hard-sphere model. A long-lived intermediate is needed.

choices.text: It explains it as electron transfer before the collision
choices.why: Electron transfer is not part of the hard-sphere model, and it is the section's explanation for stripping reactions, not for forward-and-backward scattering.

choices.text: It explains it as a rebound reaction
choices.why: A rebound reaction sends the products mostly backward. Products going both ways can't be explained by simple hard-sphere collisions at all.

explanation: There is no explanation for forward-and-backward scattering if we insist on a simple hard-sphere collision model. The section's explanation is a meta-stable intermediate: a single structure that rotates many times before it splits apart.

prompt: For a meta-stable atom-molecule intermediate to scatter its products in both forward and reverse directions, what must be true of it?

choices.text: It lasts long enough to undergo many rotations before splitting apart
It splits apart before it can complete a rotation
choices.why: A structure that breaks up at once can't reach every orientation. The section's explanation needs one that rotates many times first.

choices.text: It is formed by electron transfer at long range
choices.why: Electron transfer at long range is the mechanism of stripping reactions, which scatter mostly forward. What matters here is that the structure lives through many rotations.

choices.text: It never splits apart into products
choices.why: The products do form and scatter, so the structure must eventually split. What matters is that it lasts through many rotations before it does.

explanation: The colliding particles form a single atom-molecule structure that lasts long enough to rotate many times before it splits into products. Having turned many times, it can break apart while facing either way, so products going forward and backward are both reasonable.

prompt: Which pairing of scattering pattern and reaction type matches the section?

choices.text: Mostly backward: rebound; mostly forward: stripping
Mostly backward: stripping; mostly forward: rebound
choices.why: The names are swapped. In a rebound reaction the products bounce back; in a stripping reaction they carry on forward.

choices.text: Mostly forward: rebound; both directions: stripping
choices.why: Rebound products head backward, and products going both ways point to a long-lived intermediate. Stripping products go mostly forward.

choices.text: Mostly backward: meta-stable intermediate; both directions: rebound
choices.why: Mostly backward scattering is a rebound reaction. Products going both forward and backward point to a meta-stable intermediate.

explanation: A rebound reaction (D_2 + F) sends most products back the way they came, and a stripping reaction (K + I_2) sends them on forward. Products going both forward and backward point to a meta-stable intermediate that rotates many times before splitting.

prompt: According to the section, what made it possible to discover the rebound, stripping and meta-stable-intermediate types of reaction?

choices.text: Crossed molecular beam instruments
Measuring how concentrations change with time
choices.why: Concentration measurements give rates, not the directions in which products leave single collisions. The scattering patterns were seen with crossed molecular beams.

choices.text: Hard-sphere collision theory
choices.why: The hard-sphere model can't explain some of these patterns at all. They were discovered experimentally, with crossed molecular beam instruments.

choices.text: Measuring the equilibrium constant of each reaction
choices.why: An equilibrium constant says nothing about which way the products fly. The scattering directions were measured with crossed molecular beam instruments.

explanation: The discovery of these reaction types was made possible by crossed molecular beam instruments, which measure the directions in which the products of individual collisions scatter.
